options.a: The surgeon makes the first incision
options.b: The anesthesia provider begins preparing the patient
options.c: The patient arrives in the recovery room
options.d: The patient signs the surgical consent form

distractorExplanations.a: Incision comes after induction, so anesthesia time has already started.
distractorExplanations.c: Arrival in recovery is near the end of anesthesia time, not the start.
distractorExplanations.d: Signing consent is a pre-procedure step and is not counted as anesthesia time.

options.d: May carry forward findings or services that did not occur

options.c: To avoid billing federal programs for excluded parties
Both codes may be reported if both conditions are present

options.d: Reasons for encounters and factors influencing health

options.c: Before codes from other chapters

options.a: Medical decision making or total time on the date
options.b: The count of exam elements from the 1995 guidelines
options.c: The patient's age and new or established status
options.d: The number of diagnoses listed on the claim

distractorExplanations.b: Exam-element counting comes from the 1995/1997 guidelines, which have not set office E/M levels since 2021.
distractorExplanations.c: New versus established status picks the code family; the level within it is set by MDM or time.
distractorExplanations.d: A count of listed diagnoses is not a level criterion; MDM weighs problem complexity, not claim lines.

aapc-ccs-readiness-check-icd-015.prompt: Office/outpatient E/M level selection (current AMA framework) is based primarily on:

options.a: Staged or related procedure by the same physician (58)
options.b: Unplanned return to the OR for a related procedure
options.c: Unrelated procedure during the postoperative period (79)
options.d: Bilateral procedure performed at the same session (50)

distractorExplanations.a: Modifier 58 is for staged or planned related procedures, not unplanned returns.
distractorExplanations.c: Modifier 79 is for an unrelated procedure during the global period.
distractorExplanations.d: Modifier 50 reports a bilateral procedure, not a return to the OR.

aapc-ccs-readiness-check-pcs-001.explanation: Modifier 78 reports an unplanned return to the operating room by the same physician for a related procedure during the postoperative period. Modifier 58 covers staged or planned procedures, and 79 covers unrelated ones.

options.a: E/M codes based on time spent with the patient
options.b: ICD-10-PCS codes on professional claims
options.c: HCPCS Level II J-codes for the drugs given
options.d: CPT anesthesia codes plus base and time units

distractorExplanations.a: E/M codes report evaluation and management visits, not anesthesia services.
distractorExplanations.b: ICD-10-PCS reports inpatient facility procedures, not professional anesthesia services.
distractorExplanations.c: J-codes can report some drugs, but the anesthesia service itself uses CPT anesthesia codes.

aapc-ccs-readiness-check-pcs-003.prompt: Professional anesthesia services are typically reported with:
aapc-ccs-readiness-check-pcs-003.explanation: Anesthesia services use CPT anesthesia codes (00100–01999). Payment combines base units for the procedure, time units, and any modifying units such as physical status or qualifying circumstances, subject to payer rules.

options.a: Multiple procedures at the same session
options.b: Assistant at surgery by another surgeon
options.c: Bilateral procedure at the same session
options.d: Decision for surgery made at the E/M visit

distractorExplanations.b: Assistant surgeon services use modifier 80 (or 81, 82, or AS).
distractorExplanations.c: Bilateral procedures use modifier 50.
distractorExplanations.d: Decision for surgery uses modifier 57.

aapc-ccs-readiness-check-pcs-004.explanation: Modifier 51 flags additional procedures performed by the same provider at the same session. Payers usually reduce payment for the secondary procedures, and some codes are modifier 51 exempt.

options.a: It must be billed with every related surgery
options.b: It is not reported when integral to a larger service
options.c: It is always paid in addition to the main procedure
options.d: It is reportable only with modifier 51 attached

distractorExplanations.a: A separate procedure is not billed with related surgery when it is integral to it.
distractorExplanations.c: When integral to a larger service it is bundled, not paid in addition.
distractorExplanations.d: Modifier 51 marks multiple procedures; it does not make a separate procedure reportable.

options.a: The suture material and needle type used
options.b: The anesthetic used during the repair
options.c: Repair complexity, total length, and location
options.d: The total number of sutures that were placed

distractorExplanations.a: Suture material does not change the repair code.
distractorExplanations.b: Local anesthesia is included in the repair and does not drive code choice.
distractorExplanations.d: Suture count is not a CPT criterion; length and complexity are.

aapc-ccs-readiness-check-pcs-006.prompt: Wound repair code selection depends mainly on:

options.a: 7-day, 30-day, and 60-day globals
options.b: Globals that apply only to E/M services
options.c: A single 365-day global for all surgeries
options.d: 0-day, 10-day, and 90-day globals

distractorExplanations.a: Medicare does not use 7-, 30-, or 60-day global periods.
distractorExplanations.b: Global periods attach to surgical procedures, not E/M services.
distractorExplanations.c: Medicare has no one-year global; periods are 0, 10, or 90 days.

aapc-ccs-readiness-check-pcs-007.explanation: Medicare assigns 0-day or 10-day globals to minor procedures and 90-day globals to major procedures. Check the global period for each code in the fee schedule.

options.a: Another surgeon assisted the primary surgeon
options.b: Two surgeons each performed a distinct part
options.c: The procedure was performed on both sides
options.d: The procedure was reduced or partly completed

distractorExplanations.b: Two surgeons performing distinct parts are co-surgeons, reported with modifier 62.
distractorExplanations.c: A procedure on both sides is bilateral, modifier 50.
distractorExplanations.d: A reduced service uses modifier 52.

options.a: A bullet symbol (●) next to the code
options.b: A plus (+) symbol; never reported alone
options.c: A lightning bolt symbol next to the code
options.d: A null symbol (⊘) next to the code

distractorExplanations.a: The bullet marks a code that is new in this CPT edition, not an add-on.
distractorExplanations.c: The lightning bolt marks vaccine codes pending FDA approval.
distractorExplanations.d: The ⊘ symbol marks codes exempt from modifier 51.

options.a: All E/M visits for one year, related or not
options.b: The procedure and typical related perioperative care
options.c: Only the surgery, with each follow-up visit billed
options.d: Complications requiring a return to the OR

distractorExplanations.a: Unrelated E/M visits are billed separately (modifier 24), and globals last 0, 10, or 90 days.
distractorExplanations.c: Routine related follow-up visits are included in the package, not billed separately.
distractorExplanations.d: Complications that need a return to the OR are billed separately with modifier 78.

options.a: Diagnoses, symptoms, and reasons for encounters
options.b: Physician services and surgical procedures
options.c: Supplies, drugs, and durable medical equipment
options.d: Inpatient hospital procedures and devices

distractorExplanations.b: Physician services and procedures are reported with CPT.
distractorExplanations.c: Supplies, drugs, and DME are reported with HCPCS Level II.
distractorExplanations.d: Inpatient procedures use ICD-10-PCS, not ICD-10-CM.

aapc-ccs-readiness-check-pcs-015.prompt: ICD-10-CM codes are used primarily to report:

options.a: Guarantee that Medicaid will pay the claim
options.b: Notify the patient that Medicare may deny payment
options.c: Obtain consent to release records to Medicare
options.d: Confirm prior authorization from Medicare

distractorExplanations.a: ABNs concern Medicare noncoverage, not Medicaid payment.
distractorExplanations.c: Releasing records uses a HIPAA authorization, not an ABN.
distractorExplanations.d: An ABN is not an authorization; it only warns that Medicare may deny the service.

options.a: The service fits the clinic's schedule
options.b: The service is reasonable and needed to diagnose or treat
options.c: The patient requested the service in writing
options.d: The service is the least expensive option

distractorExplanations.a: Scheduling convenience has no bearing on medical necessity.
distractorExplanations.c: A patient request does not make a service medically necessary.
distractorExplanations.d: Necessity is about clinical need, not price.

options.a: Workplace safety and sharps injury logs
options.b: Billing fraud and false claims penalties
options.c: Use and disclosure of protected health information
options.d: Referral fees and kickback payments

distractorExplanations.a: Workplace safety and sharps logs fall under OSHA.
distractorExplanations.b: False claims are covered by the False Claims Act, not the Privacy Rule.
distractorExplanations.d: Kickbacks are covered by the Anti-Kickback Statute.

options.a: Diagnoses and reasons for visits
options.b: Inpatient hospital procedures
options.c: Physician office visits and surgeries
options.d: Drugs, supplies, DME, and some services

distractorExplanations.a: Diagnoses are reported with ICD-10-CM.
distractorExplanations.b: Inpatient procedures are coded in ICD-10-PCS.
distractorExplanations.c: Office visits and surgeries are CPT (HCPCS Level I) codes.

aapc-ccs-readiness-check-compliance-006.prompt: HCPCS Level II codes commonly report:

options.a: A patient's Medicare beneficiary number
options.b: A unique 10-digit number for health care providers
options.c: A code for where a service was performed
options.d: A payer-assigned number for each claim filed

distractorExplanations.a: Patients have Medicare Beneficiary Identifiers, not NPIs.
distractorExplanations.c: Where a service happened is the place-of-service code.
distractorExplanations.d: Payers assign claim numbers; the NPI identifies the provider.

options.a: Reporting a panel code when all tests were done
options.b: Assigning a higher E/M level than documented
options.c: Billing parts separately when one code covers all
options.d: Reporting one comprehensive code for the service

distractorExplanations.a: Using the panel code when every component test was done is correct coding.
distractorExplanations.b: Billing a higher level than documented is upcoding, not unbundling.
distractorExplanations.d: Reporting the comprehensive code is the correct alternative to unbundling.

options.a: Policies, training, auditing, and issue reporting
options.b: Annual coding productivity quotas for each coder
options.c: Automatic approval of claims by a billing vendor
options.d: Keeping audit results confidential from leadership

distractorExplanations.b: Productivity quotas are not a compliance element and can pressure coders to cut corners.
distractorExplanations.c: Compliance programs add review; they do not hand approval to a vendor.
distractorExplanations.d: Oversight requires reporting audit results to the compliance officer and leadership.

options.a: Bilateral procedure at the same session
options.b: A distinct service not normally reported together
options.c: An assistant surgeon's participation
options.d: A significant, separate E/M service that day

distractorExplanations.a: Bilateral procedures use modifier 50.
distractorExplanations.c: Assistant surgeons use modifier 80.
distractorExplanations.d: A significant, separately identifiable E/M service uses modifier 25.

aapc-ccs-readiness-check-compliance-012.prompt: Modifier 59 (or XE, XS, XP, XU) indicates:

options.a: Assign DRGs to inpatient hospital stays
options.b: Stop improper payment for code pairs billed together
options.c: Replace payers' medical necessity policies
options.d: Set the fee schedule amount for each code

distractorExplanations.a: DRGs come from the MS-DRG grouper, not NCCI.
distractorExplanations.c: NCCI edits do not replace coverage or necessity policies.
distractorExplanations.d: Fee amounts come from the physician fee schedule, not NCCI.

options.a: Review documentation and payer policy, then appeal
options.b: Resubmit the same claim without any changes
options.c: Change the diagnosis code to one that pays
options.d: Bill the patient for the full amount at once

distractorExplanations.b: Resubmitting an unchanged claim usually gets the same denial.
distractorExplanations.c: Changing codes without documentation support is fraud.
distractorExplanations.d: Billing the patient before reviewing the denial and appeal rights is premature and may be prohibited.

options.a: Guarantee that Medicare pays for the service
options.b: Replace informed consent for a procedure
options.c: Warn that Medicare may not pay for a service
options.d: Enroll the patient in a Medicare plan

distractorExplanations.a: An ABN warns of possible denial; it guarantees nothing.
distractorExplanations.b: Informed consent is separate and still required.
distractorExplanations.d: Plan enrollment is handled through Medicare, not an ABN.

options.a: Active dates, plan type, and referral needs
options.b: The patient's employer and job title
options.c: The patient's preferred appointment times
options.d: The patient's past medical history

distractorExplanations.b: Employer details may be on file but do not confirm coverage.
distractorExplanations.c: Scheduling preferences are not part of an eligibility check.
distractorExplanations.d: Medical history is clinical intake, not insurance verification.

options.a: Tell callers with chest pain it is likely anxiety
options.b: Call in an antibiotic prescription for the caller
options.c: Follow protocols and escalate urgent symptoms
options.d: Send every caller to the ER regardless of symptoms

distractorExplanations.a: MAs do not diagnose; chest pain needs urgent escalation.
distractorExplanations.b: MAs cannot prescribe or authorize prescriptions.
distractorExplanations.d: Sending everyone to the ER ignores protocol-based triage.

amt-rma-readiness-check-clinical-008.prompt: Which telephone triage action is appropriate for a medical assistant?

options.a: Track supply inventory by expiration date
options.b: Schedule patients by appointment length
options.c: Sort unpaid balances by days outstanding
options.d: Compare billed charges to the fee schedule

distractorExplanations.a: Inventory expiration tracking is not accounts receivable.
distractorExplanations.b: Scheduling is not an accounts receivable function.
distractorExplanations.d: Comparing charges to the fee schedule is charge review, not aging.

amt-rma-readiness-check-clinical-009.prompt: An accounts receivable aging report helps the office:

options.a: Strike it once, then initial, date, and correct
options.b: Cover the error with correction fluid
options.c: Remove the page and rewrite the entry
options.d: Write over the error until unreadable

distractorExplanations.b: Correction fluid hides the original entry, which is not allowed.
distractorExplanations.c: Removing pages destroys part of the legal record.
distractorExplanations.d: Obliterating the original entry makes the record look altered.

options.a: A patient pays cash for an office visit
options.b: A patient requests a copy of their records
options.c: A patient schedules an annual wellness visit
options.d: A payer requires approval before covering a service

distractorExplanations.a: Cash payment involves no payer, so no authorization is needed.
distractorExplanations.b: Records requests fall under HIPAA access rules, not payer approval.
distractorExplanations.c: Routine preventive visits generally do not need prior authorization.

options.c: Beta-2 agonist

options.a: Filter urea from the blood
options.b: Produce digestive bile
options.c: Store and concentrate bile
options.d: Secrete insulin and glucagon

distractorExplanations.a: Filtering urea is a kidney function.
distractorExplanations.b: The liver produces bile; the gallbladder stores and concentrates it.
distractorExplanations.d: Insulin and glucagon come from the pancreatic islets.

options.d: Hands visibly soiled or after C. difficile care
Palmar side of the middle or ring finger, off-center

options.b: Pancreatic beta cells

options.d: Frontal plane

options.b: At the front of the elbow
options.c: On the palm side of the wrist
options.d: At the back of the knee

options.a: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazides, or CCBs
options.b: Beta-2 agonists such as albuterol
options.c: Proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole
options.d: Antihistamines such as diphenhydramine

distractorExplanations.b: Beta-2 agonists are bronchodilators and can raise heart rate.
distractorExplanations.c: PPIs reduce stomach acid and do not lower blood pressure.
distractorExplanations.d: Antihistamines treat allergy symptoms, not hypertension.

options.a: Only patients with known infections are risky
options.b: All patients' blood and body fluids may be infectious
options.c: Gloves replace the need for hand hygiene
options.d: Only visibly ill patients need precautions

distractorExplanations.a: Standard Precautions apply to every patient, not only known infections.
distractorExplanations.c: Hand hygiene is still required after removing gloves.
distractorExplanations.d: People without symptoms can still carry bloodborne pathogens.

options.a: Reasonable emergency aid given in good faith
options.b: Care given as part of a paid clinic shift
options.c: Grossly negligent care given at an accident
options.d: Emergency care given in exchange for payment

distractorExplanations.b: Care within a paid job carries a duty to treat and is outside Good Samaritan protection.
distractorExplanations.c: Gross negligence and willful misconduct are generally not protected.
distractorExplanations.d: Expecting payment usually removes Good Samaritan protection.

amt-rma-readiness-check-law-ethics-003.prompt: A Good Samaritan statute typically protects:

options.a: A parent or guardian usually consents, with exceptions
options.b: Minors never need anyone's consent for care
options.c: School staff can consent for any student's care
options.d: Any minor may consent alone to any surgery

distractorExplanations.b: Minors generally need a parent's or guardian's consent.
distractorExplanations.c: Teachers and school staff cannot give general medical consent.
distractorExplanations.d: Minors consent alone only under specific state exceptions, such as emancipation.

options.a: Written only after the manager assigns blame
options.b: Copied into the patient's medical record
options.c: Factual, prompt, and filed per facility policy
options.d: Completed only if the patient was harmed

distractorExplanations.b: Incident reports are kept separate from the chart; the record notes only the facts of care.
distractorExplanations.d: Near misses and events without harm should also be reported.
distractorExplanations.a: Reports should be objective and timely, not blame-focused.

options.a: Protected health information (PHI)
options.b: Employee workplace safety records
options.c: Clinic financial and tax records
options.d: Public health statistics without identifiers

distractorExplanations.b: Workplace safety falls under OSHA.
distractorExplanations.c: Financial and tax records are not PHI.
distractorExplanations.d: De-identified data is not protected by the Privacy Rule.

options.a: Hear risks, benefits, and alternatives, then agree
options.b: Sign the form before any explanation is given
options.c: Agree after the provider decides for them
options.d: Be told only the benefits of the procedure

distractorExplanations.b: Signing without explanation is not informed consent.
distractorExplanations.c: Consent must be the patient's voluntary decision.
distractorExplanations.d: Risks and alternatives must also be disclosed.

amt-rma-readiness-check-law-ethics-008.prompt: Informed consent requires that the patient:

options.a: Names a person to make health decisions
options.b: Gives someone control over bank accounts
options.c: States treatment wishes if unable to communicate
options.d: Records the patient's organ donor status only

distractorExplanations.a: Naming a decision-maker is a health care proxy or durable power of attorney.
distractorExplanations.b: Control over finances is a financial power of attorney.
distractorExplanations.d: Organ donation uses a separate registry or document.

options.a: So complex only a pathologist may run it
options.b: Simple and low-risk when directions are followed
options.c: Not allowed in physician office labs
options.d: Performed only in a full reference lab

distractorExplanations.a: High-complexity tests need qualified lab personnel; waived tests are the simplest category.
distractorExplanations.c: Waived tests are commonly done in physician offices.
distractorExplanations.d: Waived tests do not require a full reference laboratory.

amt-rma-readiness-check-law-ethics-015.prompt: CLIA categorizes lab tests. A CLIA-waived test is generally:

options.a: Stabilize the pelvis, limit movement, treat for shock
options.b: Rock the pelvis repeatedly to confirm instability
options.c: Have the patient stand to test weight bearing
options.d: Apply a traction splint to the injured leg

distractorExplanations.b: Repeated rocking can dislodge clots and worsen bleeding.
distractorExplanations.c: Standing risks further injury and bleeding.
distractorExplanations.d: Traction splints are contraindicated with pelvic fractures.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-airway-001.prompt: For a suspected pelvic fracture with signs of shock, EMS should:

options.a: The patient's pain score from 0 to 10
options.b: Rule of Nines for body surface area
options.c: Glasgow Coma Scale score and pupils
options.d: Blood glucose and pulse oximetry

distractorExplanations.a: Pain does not measure burn size; deep burns can be painless.
distractorExplanations.c: GCS assesses neurologic status, not burn extent.
distractorExplanations.d: Glucose and SpO2 do not estimate burned area.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-airway-002.prompt: Burn size in the field is commonly estimated with:

options.a: Remove it to reduce infection risk
options.b: Pull it out to control the bleeding
options.c: Stabilize it in place for transport
options.d: Cut it flush with the skin surface

distractorExplanations.a: Removal can release tamponade and cause severe bleeding.
distractorExplanations.b: The object may be tamponading bleeding; pulling it out worsens hemorrhage.
distractorExplanations.d: Cutting it moves the object and can worsen tissue damage.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-airway-003.prompt: An object impaled in the thigh should generally be:

options.d: High BP, slow pulse, irregular breathing

options.a: High-risk mechanism with midline pain or deficits
options.b: Any patient involved in a motor vehicle crash
options.c: Only patients who are unconscious at the scene
options.d: Only patients who can walk at the scene

distractorExplanations.b: Crash involvement alone is not enough; selective criteria combine mechanism with findings.
distractorExplanations.c: Alert patients with midline tenderness or deficits also need restriction.
distractorExplanations.d: Being able to walk does not rule spinal injury in or out.

options.a: Push the organs back into the abdomen
options.b: Cover with moist sterile and occlusive dressings
options.c: Cover tightly with a dry adhesive bandage
options.d: Give the patient sips of water for shock

distractorExplanations.a: Replacing organs risks infection and injury; that is a surgical task.
distractorExplanations.c: Dry dressings stick to and dry out exposed organs.
distractorExplanations.d: Give nothing by mouth to a patient who may need surgery.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-airway-006.prompt: Management of an abdominal evisceration includes:

options.a: Isolated rib fracture with splinting
options.b: Hyperventilation from anxiety
options.c: Tension pneumothorax
options.d: Diaphragmatic muscle spasm

distractorExplanations.a: Rib fractures cause pain but not JVD with worsening dyspnea.
distractorExplanations.b: Anxiety does not cause JVD; assume a life threat after penetrating trauma.
distractorExplanations.d: Muscle spasm does not explain JVD and progressive distress.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-airway-007.explanation: Penetrating chest trauma with worsening dyspnea and JVD suggests tension pneumothorax. Support airway, breathing, and circulation, request ALS for decompression, and transport rapidly.

options.d: Expectant (black)

options.a: Isolated midshaft femur fracture
options.b: Pelvic fracture with leg shortening
options.c: Open tibia fracture near the ankle

distractorExplanations.b: Pelvic fractures are a contraindication for traction splints.
distractorExplanations.c: Lower-leg and ankle injuries are contraindications for traction splinting.

options.a: Place the part directly on ice
options.b: Soak the part in a container of water
options.c: Control bleeding; bag the part and keep it cool
options.d: Apply a tourniquet to the amputated part

distractorExplanations.a: Direct ice contact can freeze and destroy the tissue.
distractorExplanations.b: Soaking waterlogs tissue and lowers reattachment success.
distractorExplanations.d: A tourniquet belongs on the stump if bleeding is uncontrolled, not on the part.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-airway-010.prompt: When managing an amputation, you should:
nremt-aemt-readiness-check-airway-010.explanation: Control bleeding at the stump first. Wrap the part in a sterile dressing per protocol, seal it in a plastic bag, and keep the bag cool without direct ice contact so the tissue can possibly be reattached.

options.b: Saturation, Airway, Medications, Pulse, Level of consciousness, ECG
options.c: Scene, Allergies, Mechanism, Pulse, Last meal, Exposure
options.d: Symptoms, Airway, Mental status, Pulse, Lungs, Extremities

distractorExplanations.b: This mixes vital signs and monitoring into a list that is not SAMPLE.
distractorExplanations.c: Scene and mechanism belong to scene size-up, not the SAMPLE history.
distractorExplanations.d: Airway and lungs belong to the primary assessment, not SAMPLE.

options.a: Scene hazards and number of patients
options.b: The characteristics of pain or a symptom
options.c: Pediatric developmental milestones
options.d: Level of consciousness and orientation

distractorExplanations.a: Scene hazards are part of scene size-up.
distractorExplanations.c: Developmental milestones are not part of OPQRST.
distractorExplanations.d: Mental status is assessed with AVPU or GCS.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-airway-012.prompt: OPQRST is primarily used to assess:
nremt-aemt-readiness-check-airway-012.explanation: OPQRST stands for Onset, Provocation, Quality, Radiation, Severity, and Time. It builds a profile of the chief complaint, especially pain.

options.a: Waiting on scene to see if symptoms resolve
options.b: Giving oral aspirin before transport
options.c: Rapid transport to a stroke-capable center
options.d: Walking the patient to assess coordination

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting wastes treatment time, and symptoms may worsen.
distractorExplanations.b: Aspirin can harm a hemorrhagic stroke, and oral meds risk aspiration.
distractorExplanations.d: Walking risks falls and delays transport.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-airway-013.prompt: For a patient with stroke-like symptoms, the priority is:

options.a: Place in recovery position and observe
options.b: Ventilate with a BVM; consider naloxone
options.c: Give oral fluids to dilute the drug
options.d: Induce vomiting to remove the drug

distractorExplanations.a: Slow, shallow breathing needs assisted ventilation, not observation.
distractorExplanations.c: Never give oral fluids to an unresponsive patient.
distractorExplanations.d: Inducing vomiting risks aspiration and is not recommended.

options.a: Lower airway narrowing from asthma
options.b: Fluid in the alveoli from heart failure
options.c: A normal breath sound in young children
options.d: Partial obstruction of the upper airway

distractorExplanations.a: Lower airway narrowing produces wheezing, not stridor.
distractorExplanations.b: Fluid in the alveoli causes crackles (rales).
distractorExplanations.c: Stridor is never a normal breath sound.

options.a: It always causes the patient to vomit
options.b: It can worsen a cervical spine injury
options.c: It raises intracranial pressure
options.d: It cannot open the airway of adults

distractorExplanations.a: Head-tilt does not reliably cause vomiting.
distractorExplanations.c: The concern is spinal movement, not intracranial pressure.
distractorExplanations.d: Head-tilt/chin-lift opens adult airways well in non-trauma patients.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-pharm-006.explanation: Head-tilt/chin-lift extends the neck, which can worsen a cervical spine injury. In suspected trauma, use the jaw-thrust with manual stabilization.

options.a: Complete upper airway obstruction
options.b: Upper airway swelling at the larynx
options.c: Lower airway bronchoconstriction
options.d: Air collecting in the pleural space

distractorExplanations.a: Complete obstruction moves no air, so there is no wheeze.
distractorExplanations.b: Laryngeal swelling produces stridor.
distractorExplanations.d: Pneumothorax causes diminished breath sounds, not wheezing.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-pharm-007.prompt: Wheezing is most commonly associated with:

options.a: Oxygen by nasal cannula alone
options.b: Oxygen by nonrebreather mask alone
options.c: Abdominal thrusts until breathing improves
options.d: Positive-pressure ventilation with a BVM

distractorExplanations.a: Oxygen without ventilation cannot fix inadequate rate or depth.
distractorExplanations.b: A nonrebreather needs adequate spontaneous breathing.
distractorExplanations.c: Abdominal thrusts are for foreign-body obstruction.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-pharm-008.prompt: A patient with inadequate breathing should receive:

options.a: Respiratory distress from CHF or pulmonary edema
options.b: Complete airway obstruction by a foreign body
options.c: Respiratory arrest with no spontaneous breaths
options.d: Unresponsive patients who cannot protect the airway

distractorExplanations.b: CPAP cannot push air past a complete obstruction.
distractorExplanations.c: CPAP needs spontaneous breathing; apneic patients need ventilation.
distractorExplanations.d: CPAP requires a patient alert enough to protect the airway.

options.b: Significant hypoxemia needing urgent care

distractorExplanations.a: A bluish color signals poor oxygenation, not adequate.
distractorExplanations.c: Anemia makes cyanosis less likely to appear.

distractorExplanations.c: Five to six breaths per minute underventilates an adult.
distractorExplanations.d: Twenty breaths per minute is a pediatric-range rate and too fast for an adult with a pulse.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-pharm-013.prompt: The appropriate BVM ventilation rate for an adult with a pulse is about:

options.a: Symptomatic bradycardia with a pulse
options.b: Pulseless VF or pulseless VT
options.c: Stable chest pain with a pulse
options.d: Asystole confirmed on the monitor

distractorExplanations.a: Patients with a pulse are not defibrillated.
distractorExplanations.c: A stable patient with a pulse gets no shock.
distractorExplanations.d: Asystole is not a shockable rhythm.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-medical-001.prompt: Automated external defibrillation is indicated for:

options.a: Check a pulse for a full minute
options.b: Reanalyze the rhythm right away
options.c: Remove the pads and reassess
options.d: Resume CPR for 2 minutes, then reanalyze

distractorExplanations.a: Long pulse checks interrupt compressions.
distractorExplanations.b: Immediate reanalysis delays CPR; resume compressions first.
distractorExplanations.c: The pads stay on for the next analysis.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-medical-003.prompt: After an AED delivers a shock, the EMT should next:

options.a: Assume death since no pulse is palpable
options.b: Defibrillate over the device driveline
options.c: Follow local VAD protocols and call the VAD team
options.d: Give sublingual nitroglycerin first

distractorExplanations.a: VAD patients often lack a palpable pulse; that alone does not mean death.
distractorExplanations.b: Pads never go on the driveline or the device.
distractorExplanations.d: Nitroglycerin has no role for an unresponsive pulseless patient.

distractorExplanations.a: Pulse checks before a shock delay defibrillation; the AED has already found a shockable rhythm.
distractorExplanations.b: Turning the AED off abandons defibrillation for a shockable rhythm.
distractorExplanations.d: Remove medication patches and wipe the skin; shocking through a patch can cause burns and block current.

distractorExplanations.b: Ongoing chest pain is the indication, not a contraindication.
distractorExplanations.c: A systolic of 150 is above the usual 90–100 mm Hg minimum.
distractorExplanations.d: Prior aspirin does not prevent nitroglycerin use.

options.a: Asystole after two minutes of CPR
options.b: A sudden drop in end-tidal CO2
options.c: Fixed, dilated pupils after CPR
options.d: A palpable pulse after arrest care

distractorExplanations.a: Asystole means there is no circulation.
distractorExplanations.b: ROSC causes a sudden rise, not a drop, in end-tidal CO2.
distractorExplanations.c: Fixed, dilated pupils suggest poor brain perfusion, not ROSC.

distractorExplanations.c: Anxiety is a diagnosis of exclusion after ACS is ruled out.
